note.label: The Superiority of the Chosen People

precepts.why:
In Exodus 1 the new king says “the people of the children of Israel are more and mightier than we: Come on, let us deal wisely with them.” The Egyptians were tall and strong, yet they said the Hebrews were mightier; something had happened for them to know it. They could not destroy us head on, so they set up institutions of oppression to keep us beneath them. There is nothing new under the sun, and Jim Crow was already around in Joseph’s time.

Genesis 43:32: “And they set on for him by himself, and for them by themselves, and for the Egyptians, which did eat with him, by themselves: because the Egyptians might not eat bread with the Hebrews; for that is an abomination unto the Egyptians.”

Joseph had status. He was second over Egypt, the governor, the vizier, and still he was not granted the privileges of a full-blooded Egyptian. His Egyptian servants could not sit with him; they had their own table and he had his. He was a resource they could use, because his God gave him the dreams that kept them from famine, but he could not sit at their table because he was a Hebrew. It was an abomination for an Egyptian to eat with a Hebrew.

That is Jim Crow: Egyptians sit here, Hebrews sit there; whites sit here, coloreds sit there. The same people who used Joseph’s wisdom kept him apart, and the same thinking later dealt wisely with us in Egypt and in America.

note.label: The Superiority of the Chosen People

precepts.why:
Did it change after Joseph’s table? No. When his family came down, Joseph told them what to say to Pharaoh. “the men are shepherds, for their trade hath been to feed cattle;” and when Pharaoh asks, “What is your occupation?” they were to answer: “Thy servants’ trade hath been about cattle from our youth even until now, both we, and also our fathers: that ye may dwell in the land of Goshen; for every shepherd is an abomination unto the Egyptians.”

The Israelites were known as shepherds. Because of the war with the shepherd kings before Joseph arrived, the Egyptians hated shepherds, so the Israelites were despised twice over, as Hebrews and as shepherds.

So Israel was placed in Goshen, an isolated area away from the Egyptians. Egyptians and shepherds could not live in the same vicinity, which means there were no Egyptians living among us to put their blood into ours. That is segregation; that is redlining. It is nothing new.

That separation is the ground Exodus 1 grows out of. A people set apart, more and mightier than their masters, “dealt wisely” with: taskmasters over them, building Pithom and Raamses, serving “with rigour” in mortar, brick and “all manner of service in the field.” The same pattern followed us into America: set apart, built the Capitol and the White House, worked the fields.

note.label: Why They Hated US: Walking in the Footsteps of the Persecuted

precepts.why:
Pharaoh’s crafty counsel had a plan behind it, and here it is: “When ye do the office of a midwife to the Hebrew women, and see them upon the stools; if it be a son, then ye shall kill him: but if it be a daughter, then she shall live.”

What they were hoping for was to run into Hebrew women who hated themselves and hated their people, so their plan could be executed. They were doing it by proxy of the midwives, hoping the midwives felt the way the rebellious Israelites felt coming out of Egypt: we miss the garlics, we miss the leeks, take us back, we like being a slave. “But the midwives feared God, and did not as the king of Egypt commanded them, but saved the men children alive.” That means the midwives loved their people. They feared God, and the way they showed it was that they loved their people.

The enemies of Israel have always capitalized off of our hatred of ourselves. What was commanded in Egypt is what abortion has evolved into: make the babies that come out of Israelite wombs vanish. Now the black mind has been so twisted and perverted that they do not even have to put out an edict that says kill the children. The black woman will do it herself, and she is already doing it by the millions. That is a genocide in itself.

That is why we must be the ones to correct this, to highlight it, illuminate it, and set the nation back in order: restore the love of ourselves and the fear of God, and show that the enemy hates us.

That curse was on us in ancient Egypt: the Egyptians were over us and we were the bottom of society, the same way the nations are above us today and we are the bottom of society. note.label: Passover Class: Exodus From America Modern Day Egypt

precepts.why:
Exodus 1:11 says “they did set over them taskmasters to afflict them with their burdens.” Deuteronomy 28 names that as a curse: “The stranger that is within thee shall get up above thee very high; and thou shalt come down very low. He shall lend to thee, and thou shalt not lend to him: he shall be the head, and thou shalt be the tail.”

The strangers are the people that were amongst us. They get above us very high, and we come down very low. To be above us means they rule and tell us what to do, and another name for that is taskmaster.

That curse was on us in ancient Egypt: the Egyptians were over us, and we were on the bottom of society. It is the same way the so-called white man and the nations are above us today, and we are the bottom of society. The taskmasters today are the governors, the politicians, the police officers, the FBI agents, people set to keep us in check and keep us in order, with laws like Jim Crow and the black codes to keep us low. On the cotton field there was always a white overseer to make sure we did the work, or you got your ass whooped. Today your taskmaster is your boss.

What was done to us in ancient Egypt is what was done to us in America. That is why this place is spiritually called Egypt.

note.label: Passover Class: Exodus From America Modern Day Egypt

precepts.why:
“And they built for Pharaoh treasure cities, Pithom and Raamses.” We built cities in ancient Egypt, and it is the same thing here in America. Deuteronomy 28:30 lists it among the curses: “Thou shalt betroth a wife, and another man shall lie with her: thou shalt build an house, and thou shalt not dwell therein: thou shalt plant a vineyard, and shalt not gather the grapes thereof.”

In ancient Egypt we built cities and houses, and we did not build them for ourselves; we built them for the Egyptians. We were a commodity, and they did not look at us as human. America did the same.

What house did we build here in America and could not dwell in it? The White House. Construction began in 1792 in Washington D.C., and hundreds of enslaved people rented from plantation owners quarried the stone, cut the timber and laid the bricks, dawn to dusk, with no wages, whipped if they slowed down. Most are not even named in the records, just negro hired. When it was finished in 1800 and President Adams moved in, the enslaved workers were sent back to the plantations with no credit and no freedom, and for the next 65 years more enslaved people worked there. Some of you thought the white man built that.

We built cities in Egypt and did not dwell in them, and we built the White House and cannot dwell in it. The same curse, in ancient Egypt and in spiritual Egypt.

Exodus 1:14 says “they made their lives bitter with hard bondage, in morter, and in brick, and in all manner of service in the field”. We were in the fields in ancient Egypt; we were not just building pyramids. They had us doing plantation work and cropping there too. Deuteronomy 28:16 is that curse: “Cursed shalt thou be in the city, and cursed shalt thou be in the field.”

The same way ancient Egypt made us slaves and worked us in the fields with all manner of service, in America that curse also fell upon us. We were cursed in the cotton field, in the sugar cane field, in the tobacco field, with five year olds and two year olds picking cotton. Our lives were made bitter, and that is why we eat the bitter herbs at Passover: they represent our lives being bitter in Egypt.

And all manner of service: we were their servants, cooking their food, watching their kids, entertaining them. Sing, this Hebrew got a good voice, sing me one of the songs of Zion. That is what we do here in Babylon. Some of you drive a bus, fix the road, drive a taxi cab: servant jobs, and you don't see it. We have been slaves so long we got comfortable with the jobs they give us. We are kings and priests; we are not supposed to serve any nation. Our job is to serve God.

Read the curses of Deuteronomy 28 and then read what happened to us in ancient Egypt, and you will see they are the same. America is spiritual Egypt.

precepts.why:
Exodus 1:12 says “the more they afflicted them, the more they multiplied and grew. And they were grieved because of the children of Israel.” No matter how much they afflicted us, we kept multiplying and growing. And what does it mean that the Egyptians were grieved because of us? They were mad; they were angry.

Leviticus 26:17 explains it: “And I will set my face against you, and ye shall be slain before your enemies: they that hate you shall reign over you; and ye shall flee when none pursueth you.” To be grieved because of the children of Israel means they hated us, and they that hated us reigned over us.

The same way the ancient Egyptians hated us, the so-called white man hated us when we were brought here as slaves. So “the Egyptians made the children of Israel to serve with rigour”: they did not play with us. In ancient Egypt they beat the hell out of us with whips, and in America the same: runaways caught and whooped, lynchings, and still lynching us. Not only America but all the lands we were scattered into are Egypt, but this is the main one, Mystery Babylon.

precepts.why:
“Now there arose up a new king over Egypt, which knew not Joseph”. This new king set taskmasters over Israel to afflict them with burdens, and then went further: “And Pharaoh charged all his people, saying, Every son that is born ye shall cast into the river, and every daughter ye shall save alive”.

That is gator bait. They sacrificed our baby boys in the river to Sobek, the gator god. The white man did the exact same thing to us in the Florida Everglades: put our babies in a net, wait for the alligator to bite, pull the gator out and make shoes and bags out of him. Egypt did it to us first. They killed the males and kept the women alive, because the women do not produce the nation; the man does.

That decree is why Moses was hidden three months and laid in an ark of bulrushes by the river's brink, and why everything that follows was done in secret. When Pharaoh's daughter came down to the river in Exodus 2:5 and found the ark, she found one of the very sons her father had ordered cast into the river.

precepts.text: And Joseph died, and all his brethren, and all that generation; Judah ended his days in Egypt.
precepts.point: Judah's line went down into Egypt in the end, and Judah died there with his brethren; and Joseph died, and all his brethren, and all that generation.

note.label: Genesis 38: Judah and Tamar

precepts.why:
“And Joseph died, and all his brethren, and all that generation.” Judah was among those brethren. Judah’s line, Pharez and Zarah with him, went down into Egypt in the end, and Judah ended his days there, dying in Egypt with his brethren.

So the twins born here, Pharez who broke forth first and Zarah with the scarlet thread upon his hand, were the beginning of the line of Judah that carried on into Egypt after Judah and all that generation were gone.

precepts.text: A new king which knew not Joseph set taskmasters over Israel to afflict them with their burdens, and they built for Pharaoh treasure cities.
precepts.point: There arose up a new king over Egypt which knew not Joseph; fearing that the children of Israel were more and mightier than they, Egypt set over them taskmasters to afflict them with their burdens, and they built for Pharaoh the treasure cities, Pithom and Raamses.

note.label: Deuteronomy 26: The Firstfruits Confession and a Peculiar People

precepts.why:
“And the Egyptians evil entreated us, and afflicted us, and laid upon us hard bondage”. Exodus tells how it began: “Now there arose up a new king over Egypt, which knew not Joseph. And he said unto his people, Behold, the people of the children of Israel are more and mightier than we: Come on, let us deal wisely with them; lest they multiply, and it come to pass, that, when there falleth out any war, they join also unto our enemies, and fight against us, and so get them up out of the land.”

Fearing that the children of Israel were more and mightier than they, Egypt dealt with them: “Therefore they did set over them taskmasters to afflict them with their burdens. And they built for Pharaoh treasure cities, Pithom and Raamses.” The taskmasters and the burdens are the affliction, and building Pithom and Raamses for Pharaoh is the hard bondage the confession speaks of.

precepts.text: The children of Israel that came into Egypt with Jacob are named, the same sons listed here.
precepts.point: The nations call us a minority and divide us by many labels so they can deal wisely with us, but we are not a minority, and the Most High promised to multiply our seed like the stars of heaven and the sand of the sea.

note.label: 1 Chronicles 2: The Sons of Israel and the Line of Judah

precepts.why:
“Now these are the names of the children of Israel, which came into Egypt; every man and his household came with Jacob.” These are the same sons listed in Chronicles: “Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun, Dan, Joseph, and Benjamin, Naphtali, Gad, and Asher.”

These are the sons of Jacob that came into Egypt, and we carry their name, their lineage, and their descent from the twelve tribes of Israel.

precepts.text: The nation dealt wisely with Israel and made their lives bitter with hard bondage and service.
precepts.point: This place is spiritual Egypt. The nations dealt wisely with us and put us to hard labor and bondage, and we are the essential workers on the front line.

note.label: Psalm 44: We Got Not the Land by Our Own Sword

precepts.why:
“Though thou hast sore broken us in the place of dragons”. This place is spiritual Egypt. In Egypt they said, “Come on, let us deal wisely with them; lest they multiply”, and “they did set over them taskmasters to afflict them with their burdens.” “And the Egyptians made the children of Israel to serve with rigour: And they made their lives bitter with hard bondage, in morter, and in brick, and in all manner of service in the field”.

The nations have dealt wisely with us the same way and put us to hard labour and bondage; we are the essential workers on the front line. That is how the Most High brought down our heart with labour, sore broken in the place of dragons and covered with the shadow of death. But “the more they afflicted them, the more they multiplied and grew.”

precepts.point: There is little Benjamin with their ruler, the princes of Judah and their council, the princes of Zebulun and the princes of Naphtali. These are the tribes of Israel, the sons of Jacob whose name was changed to Israel.

note.label: Psalm 68: Let God Arise

precepts.why:
“There is little Benjamin with their ruler, the princes of Judah and their council, the princes of Zebulun, and the princes of Naphtali.” These are the tribes of Israel, the sons of Jacob, whose name was changed to Israel. “Now these are the names of the children of Israel, which came into Egypt; every man and his household came with Jacob. Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, and Benjamin, Dan, and Naphtali, Gad, and Asher.”

Benjamin, Judah, Zebulun and Naphtali in the psalm are these same sons who came into Egypt with Jacob. Bless ye God in the congregations, even the Lord, from the fountain of Israel: the congregations are these tribes, with the singers before and the players on instruments after, and the damsels playing with timbrels among them like a marching band.

precepts.text: The Egyptians dealt subtly with Israel and turned to hate them.
precepts.point: He smote all the firstborn, the chief of all their strength. The firstborn is the chief of one's strength, as Reuben was Jacob's strength before he lost it.

note.label: Psalm 105: Remember His Marvelous Works from Abraham to the Exodus

precepts.why:
“He turned their heart to hate his people, to deal subtilly with his servants.” Exodus shows how: “there arose up a new king over Egypt, which knew not Joseph”, and he said, “Behold, the people of the children of Israel are more and mightier than we: Come on, let us deal wisely with them; lest they multiply”.

That is the Most High increasing his people greatly and making them stronger than their enemies, just as the psalm says, and the Egyptians fearing it. “Therefore they did set over them taskmasters to afflict them with their burdens. And they built for Pharaoh treasure cities, Pithom and Raamses. But the more they afflicted them, the more they multiplied and grew.”

“And the Egyptians made the children of Israel to serve with rigour: And they made their lives bitter with hard bondage, in morter, and in brick, and in all manner of service in the field”. Israel came into Egypt and Jacob sojourned in the land of Ham, and the Egyptians dealt subtilly with Israel and turned to hate them. Then he sent Moses his servant and Aaron whom he had chosen, with his signs and wonders in the land of Ham.

precepts.text: Pharaoh charged all his people to cast every son into the river, the same attempt to cut off a deliverer before he could grow.
precepts.point: Herod slays all the children in Bethlehem from two years old and under. This is the same pattern as Egypt, where the ruler killed the young children to stop a deliverer from rising.

note.label: Matthew 2: The Wise Men, Herod's Fear, and the Flight into Egypt

precepts.why:
When Herod saw that he was mocked of the wise men, he “sent forth, and slew all the children that were in Bethlehem, and in all the coasts thereof, from two years old and under”.

This is the same pattern as Egypt, where the ruler killed the young children to stop a deliverer from rising. “And Pharaoh charged all his people, saying, Every son that is born ye shall cast into the river, and every daughter ye shall save alive.” Pharaoh had every son cast into the river to cut off the deliverer before he could grow. Herod slew the children of Bethlehem two years old and under for the same reason, to cut off the child born King of the Jews before he could grow. The ruler changes; the attempt is the same.
